1:1.t: Ezra opens where 2 Chronicles closes (2 Chronicles 36:22-23); the two passages are nearly word for word.

1:4.t: "Any survivor": the KJV's "whosoever remaineth", meaning any Israelite left from the exile.

1:9.t: "Dishes": the KJV's "chargers", large platters. "Knives": the Hebrew word is rare; some take it as pans or censers.

1:10.t: "Of a lesser kind": the KJV's "of a second sort".

1:11.t: The items in verses 9-10 add up to 2,499, not 5,400. The lists may give only the chief items; 1 Esdras 2:13-14 has different figures.

2:1.t: This list appears again, with some differences in names and numbers, in Nehemiah 7:6-73.

2:2.t: This Nehemiah and this Mordecai are not the Nehemiah of the book of Nehemiah or the Mordecai of Esther.

2:21.t: "People of" a town: the KJV says "children of" or "men of"; with a place name it means the people from that town.

2:25.t: Modern spellings: Kiriath-arim, Geba, Michmash, Bethel, Bethlehem, Pashhur, Meunim, Temah, Pochereth-hazzebaim, Tel-harsha, Hakkoz. The KJV spells them Kirjath-arim, Gaba, Michmas, Beth-el, Beth-lehem, Pashur, Mehunim, Thamah, Pochereth of Zebaim, Tel-harsa, Koz.

2:38.t: Modern spellings: Kiriath-arim, Geba, Michmash, Bethel, Bethlehem, Pashhur, Meunim, Temah, Pochereth-hazzebaim, Tel-harsha, Hakkoz. The KJV spells them Kirjath-arim, Gaba, Michmas, Beth-el, Beth-lehem, Pashur, Mehunim, Thamah, Pochereth of Zebaim, Tel-harsa, Koz.

2:50.t: Modern spellings: Kiriath-arim, Geba, Michmash, Bethel, Bethlehem, Pashhur, Meunim, Temah, Pochereth-hazzebaim, Tel-harsha, Hakkoz. The KJV spells them Kirjath-arim, Gaba, Michmas, Beth-el, Beth-lehem, Pashur, Mehunim, Thamah, Pochereth of Zebaim, Tel-harsa, Koz.

2:61.t: Modern spellings: Kiriath-arim, Geba, Michmash, Bethel, Bethlehem, Pashhur, Meunim, Temah, Pochereth-hazzebaim, Tel-harsha, Hakkoz. The KJV spells them Kirjath-arim, Gaba, Michmas, Beth-el, Beth-lehem, Pashur, Mehunim, Thamah, Pochereth of Zebaim, Tel-harsa, Koz.

2:42.t: "Gatekeepers": the KJV's "porters", the Levites who guarded the temple gates.

2:43.t: "Temple servants": the KJV's "Nethinims". The Hebrew nethinim already is a plural and means "those given", people given to serve in the temple (see 8:20).

2:62.t: "Unclean": the KJV's "polluted", meaning not fit to serve as priests.

2:63.t: "The governor": the KJV keeps the Persian title, "the Tirshatha", a title of honor for a governor. Nehemiah 8:9 gives it to Nehemiah. "Urim and Thummim": objects kept by the high priest for learning God's will (Exodus 28:30).

2:64.t: The separate numbers in this chapter add up to 29,818, fewer than the total of 42,360. The total may include people not listed by family.

2:69.t: KJV: "threescore and one thousand drams of gold, and five thousand pound of silver". The "dram" is the Persian gold coin called the daric (about 8.4 grams of gold). The "pound" is the mina, about 570 grams.

3:4.t: "Feast of Shelters": the KJV's "feast of tabernacles", when the people lived in shelters made of branches (Leviticus 23:42).

3:6.t: Some KJV printings add "was not yet founded" after this verse; it is a margin note, not part of the text.

3:7.t: Sidon: the KJV spells it Zidon.

3:9.t: "The descendants of Judah": the Hebrew is "the sons of Judah", perhaps a mistake for Hodaviah (2:40), since the Hebrew names are alike.

3:11.t: "They sang in turn": the KJV's "by course", taking turns in two groups.

"His steadfast love" (Hebrew hesed): the KJV's "mercy". hesed is loyal, committed love that keeps its promises, especially within a covenant; no single English word covers it, and the KJV uses "mercy", "kindness" and "lovingkindness". See Genesis 24:27. The words "He is good; His steadfast love lasts forever" are the refrain of Psalm 136 and other psalms. "Steadfast love" is used for hesed in Ezra and Nehemiah because the setting is God's faithfulness to His covenant; at 7:28 and 9:9 the KJV has "mercy".

4:2.t: Esarhaddon: the KJV spells it Esar-haddon. Assyria: the KJV's "Assur".

4:6.t: Ahasuerus is the Hebrew form of the Persian name the Greeks wrote as Xerxes. The KJV form is kept here and in Esther.
These verses step forward in time from the days of Cyrus and Darius to later kings (Ahasuerus, Artaxerxes) to show that the opposition went on for years. Verse 24 returns to the time of Darius.

4:7.t: "In the Aramaic script and in the Aramaic language": the KJV's "in the Syrian tongue, and interpreted in the Syrian tongue". Aramaic was the common language of the Persian empire.

4:8.t: "Commanding officer": the KJV's "chancellor". The Aramaic title means "master of decree", a high official.

and 7:12-26 Aramaic: these sections are written in Aramaic, not Hebrew. They are mostly copies of official letters and decrees, kept in the language of the Persian government, with the story between them told in Aramaic too. The book returns to Hebrew at 6:19 and 7:27. The KJV does not show the change; we note it here.

4:9.t: "Commanding officer": the KJV's "chancellor". The Aramaic title means "master of decree", a high official.

The KJV takes these words as names of peoples, and we follow it. Some of them may be official titles instead (judges, envoys, officials). "People of Erech" and "people of Susa": the KJV's "Archevites" and "Susanchites".

4:17.t: "Commanding officer": the KJV's "chancellor". The Aramaic title means "master of decree", a high official.

4:10.t: Osnappar: the KJV spells it Asnappar. He is probably the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal. "And now": the KJV's "and at such a time", a phrase that opens the body of a letter.
and following "The region west of the Euphrates": the KJV's "this side the river" or "beyond the river". This was the Persian province west of the Euphrates, seen from Persia as "Beyond the River".

4:14.t: "We eat the salt of the palace": the KJV's "we have maintenance from the king's palace". The Aramaic says "we eat the salt", that is, we are in the king's pay and owe him loyalty.

5:1.t: "Who was over them": the KJV's "even unto them". The Aramaic can mean the God whose name was over them.

5:3.t: Tattenai and Shethar-bozenai: the KJV spells them Tatnai and Shethar-boznai.
"Finish this structure": the KJV's "make up this wall". The Aramaic word is rare and may mean the structure or its woodwork.

5:6.t: Tattenai and Shethar-bozenai: the KJV spells them Tatnai and Shethar-boznai.
"Officials": the KJV's "Apharsachites", which it takes as a people; the word is probably a Persian title.

6:6.t: Tattenai and Shethar-bozenai: the KJV spells them Tatnai and Shethar-boznai.
"Officials": the KJV's "Apharsachites", which it takes as a people; the word is probably a Persian title.

6:13.t: Tattenai and Shethar-bozenai: the KJV spells them Tatnai and Shethar-boznai.

5:9.t: "Finish this structure": the KJV's "make up this wall". The Aramaic word is rare and may mean the structure or its woodwork.

5:4.t: "Then we asked them": as in the KJV. The Aramaic says "we", which is odd in the middle of a report; the Greek Old Testament reads "they", and many modern Bibles follow it.

5:8.t: "Judah": the KJV's "Judea". The Aramaic is Yehud, the Persian name of the province.

5:14.t: "Governor": the Aramaic word is pechah, the same title given to Tattenai in 5:3. Some think Sheshbazzar is another name for Zerubbabel; others take him to be an earlier leader.

6:2.t: Ecbatana: the KJV's "Achmetha", the summer capital of the Persian kings in Media. "Scroll": the KJV's "roll".

6:3.t: KJV: "threescore cubits" high and wide. The decree gives no length.

6:11.t: "Hanged on it": as in the KJV. The Aramaic means to be lifted up and fastened on the beam, which may mean impaled.

6:14.t: Artaxerxes reigned after the temple was finished. He is named because he later supported the temple (7:15-24).

6:15.t: Adar is the twelfth month, February to March. The sixth year of Darius was 516 BC.

6:18.t: "Divisions" and "groups": the KJV's "divisions" and "courses", the rotation of duties.

6:22.t: "The king of Assyria": the Persian king is meant. He ruled the lands that had once been Assyria.

7:6.t: "A scribe well trained": the KJV's "a ready scribe", skilled and quick. A scribe here is a scholar of the law, not only a copyist.

7:9.t: The journey of about 1,450 kilometers took four months.

7:12.t: "Perfect peace. And now": the KJV's "perfect peace, and at such a time", a phrase that opens the body of a letter. See 4:10.

"The God of heaven": a title used mainly in the Persian period (Ezra, Nehemiah, Daniel). It was a name Persian officials understood and could use themselves, and it presents the God of Israel as the God over all, not one god among many. In Hebrew it is Elohe hashamayim; in the Aramaic passages, Elah shemaya.

7:17.t: "Grain offerings": the KJV's "meat offerings", in the old sense of food.

7:22.t: KJV: "an hundred talents of silver", "an hundred measures of wheat" (the cor), "an hundred baths of wine", "an hundred baths of oil".

7:28.t: Here the book changes from speaking of Ezra to Ezra speaking in his own voice ("me", "I"); this goes on to the end of chapter 9.

8:2.t: Hattush, of the line of Shecaniah: the verse division in the KJV is unclear here; 1 Chronicles 3:22 lists Hattush among the descendants of Shecaniah. Parosh: the KJV spells it Pharosh here.

8:3.t: Shecaniah: the KJV spells it Shechaniah.

8:5.t: Shecaniah: the KJV spells it Shechaniah.

"The son of Jahaziel", "the son of Josiphiah": the man's own name is missing from the Hebrew. The Greek Old Testament reads "Shecaniah the son of Jahaziel" from the descendants of Zattu and "Shelomith the son of Josiphiah" from the descendants of Bani.

10:2.t: Shecaniah: the KJV spells it Shechaniah.
and following "Foreign women": the KJV's "strange wives", meaning women from other nations.
"Hope" (Hebrew miqveh): the word can also mean a gathering of water, a pool. Here it means a ground for expecting good, something to rest on.

8:4.t: Eliehoenai: the KJV spells it Elihoenai.

8:10.t: "The son of Jahaziel", "the son of Josiphiah": the man's own name is missing from the Hebrew. The Greek Old Testament reads "Shecaniah the son of Jahaziel" from the descendants of Zattu and "Shelomith the son of Josiphiah" from the descendants of Bani.

8:13.t: "Those who came later": the KJV's "the last sons", perhaps meaning these were the last of that family to return.

8:15.t: Ahava was a town or canal in Babylonia; the place is not known.

8:21.t: Ahava was a town or canal in Babylonia; the place is not known.
"Humble ourselves": the KJV's "afflict ourselves", meaning to fast and deny oneself.

8:31.t: Ahava was a town or canal in Babylonia; the place is not known.

8:26.t: KJV: "six hundred and fifty talents of silver, and silver vessels an hundred talents, and of gold an hundred talents". These are very large amounts, about 22 metric tons of silver and 3.4 tons of gold.

8:27.t: KJV: "twenty basons of gold, of a thousand drams"; the dram is the gold daric, a Persian coin of about 8.4 grams of gold (see 2:69). "Fine polished bronze": the KJV's "fine copper".

8:36.t: "Satraps": the KJV's "lieutenants", the Persian governors of large provinces.

9:1.t: "Detestable practices": the KJV's "abominations", things God hates, especially idol worship.

9:11.t: "Detestable practices": the KJV's "abominations", things God hates, especially idol worship.
The prophets are quoted in summary; the words echo Deuteronomy 7:1-3 and Leviticus 18:24-30.

9:14.t: "Detestable practices": the KJV's "abominations", things God hates, especially idol worship.

9:2.t: "Unfaithfulness": the KJV's "trespass". The Hebrew maal means breaking faith, betraying a trust.

"Holy offspring" (Hebrew zera haqqodesh, "holy seed"): zera is a collective singular, so it can mean one descendant or many (see Genesis 3:15). Here it means the people set apart for God, not a claim about bloodline. The concern of chapters 9-10 is faithfulness to God, as 9:1 and 9:11 show: the danger named is the "detestable practices" of other peoples, that is, their gods.

9:3.t: "Tunic and cloak": the KJV's "garment and mantle". "In shock": the KJV's "astonied", stunned, appalled.

9:8.t: "A firm hold": the KJV's "a nail". The Hebrew word means a tent peg, driven in to hold a tent firmly in place.

"Remnant", "survivors" (Hebrew sheerit and peletah): sheerit is what is left over after a disaster, and peletah is those who escaped it. The prophets use these words for the people God keeps for Himself after judgment (Isaiah 10:20-22). Ezra uses both to say that the returned exiles live only by God's mercy and could lose even that.

9:9.t: "A protecting wall": the KJV's "a wall". The Hebrew word means a fence or wall around a vineyard, a picture of protection, not the city wall, which was built later under Nehemiah.

10:10.t: and following "Foreign women": the KJV's "strange wives", meaning women from other nations.

10:3.t: "Send away": the KJV's "put away", meaning to divorce.

10:8.t: "Cut off": the KJV's "separated", put out of the community.

10:9.t: The ninth month (Kislev) is November to December, the rainy season.

10:15.t: "Were appointed over this matter": the KJV's "were employed about this matter". The Hebrew can also mean that these men "stood against" the plan, and many modern Bibles read it that way. Jahzeiah: the KJV spells it Jahaziah.

10:19.t: "Gave their hand in pledge": the KJV's "gave their hands", a gesture of solemn promise.

10:22.t: Modern spellings: Nethanel, Izziah, Mijamin, Malchijah, Elijah, Bezalel, Isshijah, Mattattah, Cheluhi, Jaasu, Azarel, Jaddai. The KJV spells them Nethaneel, Jeziah, Miamin, Malchiah, Eliah, Bezaleel, Ishijah, Mattathah, Chelluh, Jaasau, Azareel, Jadau.

10:44.t: "And some of them had wives by whom they had children": as in the KJV. The Hebrew is difficult; the book ends without saying how the matter was settled for each family.

6:16.t: "Dedication" (Aramaic hanukkah): the same word later names the Jewish feast of Hanukkah, which remembers the rededication of the temple in 164 BC.

7:10.t: "To study" (Hebrew darash): the KJV's "to seek". The word means to search out, inquire, and it is the root of later Jewish words for the study and interpretation of Scripture (midrash). Ezra's order, study, then do, then teach, is the point of the verse.

9:13.t: "Remnant", "survivors" (Hebrew sheerit and peletah): sheerit is what is left over after a disaster, and peletah is those who escaped it. The prophets use these words for the people God keeps for Himself after judgment (Isaiah 10:20-22). Ezra uses both to say that the returned exiles live only by God's mercy and could lose even that.

9:15.t: "Righteous" (Hebrew tsaddiq): being right, in the right before God and true to His standards (see Genesis 15:6). Here God's righteousness is the reason for His judgment and also for His keeping a remnant; Ezra does not plead innocence but appeals to God's character.
